title: Projection matrices
summary: The orthogonal projection onto the column space of a full-column-rank matrix A is P=A(A^T A)^{-1}A^T. It is symmetric and idempotent, with eigenvalues 0 and 1 only, and trace equal to rank.
intuition:
This lesson is about the matrix of an orthogonal projection, not about the picture of dropping a perpendicular. The picture, the formula $\mathrm{proj}_u v$, and the normal equations live in the projections lesson. What belongs here is the single matrix $P$ that carries every vector in $\mathbb{R}^m$ onto a chosen subspace.

If the subspace is the column space of a real $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with independent columns, that matrix is $P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$. Full column rank is the hypothesis that makes $A^\top A$ square and invertible. The product is an $m\times m$ matrix. Applying $P$ to a vector $b$ returns the point of the column space closest to $b$. Computing that vector for one $b$ is geometry; the projections lesson does it from the normal equations. The two routes agree.

Three algebraic facts follow from the formula, and they are the ones a question asks you to recognise. First, $P$ is symmetric: $P^\top=P$. Second, $P$ is idempotent: $P^2=P$. Projecting a vector that is already in the subspace does nothing. Third, the only eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$, because $P^2-P=0$ leaves no room for any other root, and $P$ is diagonalizable. The trace counts the eigenvalues equal to $1$, which is the dimension of the column space, so $\mathrm{trace}(P)=\mathrm{rank}(P)$. Symmetry is part of the definition of an orthogonal projection. An idempotent matrix that is not symmetric projects along a slanted direction; that object is the idempotent-matrix lesson, and it is not this $P$.

definitions.body: A square real matrix $P$ is the matrix of an orthogonal projection when $P^\top=P$ and $P^2=P$. Equivalently, $P$ is symmetric and idempotent. The image of $P$ is the subspace being projected onto.

If the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, $P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of $A$. The hypothesis is full column rank, so that $A^\top A$ is invertible.
Every eigenvalue of an orthogonal projection matrix is $0$ or $1$. Counting multiplicity, $\mathrm{trace}(P)$ equals the number of eigenvalues equal to $1$, which equals $\mathrm{rank}(P)$.

formulas.name: Orthogonal projection
formulas.note: $A$ has full column rank. Then $P^2=P=P^\top$. Eigenvalues are $0$ or $1$, and $\mathrm{trace}(P)=\mathrm{rank}(P)$.

formulas.name: Orthonormal columns
formulas.note: The inverse in the general formula is the identity precisely when the columns are already orthonormal.

properties: $P^2=P=P^\top$ for the orthogonal projection onto the column space of a full-column-rank matrix.
The only possible eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$. A vector in the column space has eigenvalue $1$; a vector orthogonal to every column has eigenvalue $0$.
$\mathrm{trace}(P)=\mathrm{rank}(P)$. For a projection onto a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$, the trace is $k$ and the nullity is $m-k$.
$I-P$ is the orthogonal projection onto the orthogonal complement of the column space. It is also symmetric and idempotent.
If the columns of $A$ are orthonormal, the formula collapses to $P=AA^\top$. It does not collapse that far for a general full-rank $A$.
Symmetry is required. Idempotence alone does not make an orthogonal projection; the idempotent-matrix lesson has a non-symmetric example.

examples.title: Projection onto the line through $(1,1,0)$
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$. Build $P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$ and check $P^2=P=P^\top$, the trace, and the eigenvalues.
steps: The product of the integer matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ with itself is $2M$, so $P^2=(M/2)^2=M/2=P$. Also $M$ is symmetric, so $P^\top=P$. The trace is $\tfrac12+\tfrac12+0=1$, and the single column of $A$ is independent, so the rank is $1$.
Directly, $P(1,1,0)^\top=(1,1,0)^\top$, while $P(1,-1,0)^\top=0$ and $P(0,0,1)^\top=0$. The eigenvalues are $1,0,0$. Their sum is the trace.
examples.answer: $P=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. It satisfies $P^2=P=P^\top$, its eigenvalues are $1,0,0$, and $\mathrm{trace}(P)=\mathrm{rank}(P)=1$.

examples.title: A rank-$2$ projection in $\mathbb{R}^3$
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, which has full column rank. The formula produces $P=\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&1\\-1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Verify $P^2=P=P^\top$ and $\mathrm{trace}(P)=\mathrm{rank}(P)$. For $b=(1,1,0)^\top$, name $Pb$ and leave the geometry to the projections lesson.
steps: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&1\\-1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, so $P=M/3$. Matrix multiplication gives $M^2=3M$. Therefore $P^2=M^2/9=3M/9=M/3=P$.
$M$ is symmetric, so $P^\top=P$. The diagonal sum of $M$ is $2+2+2=6$, hence $\mathrm{trace}(P)=2$. The two columns of $A$ are independent, so $\mathrm{rank}(P)=2$.

Apply $P$ to $b=(1,1,0)^\top$: $Mb=(1,1,2)^\top$ and $Pb=\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac23\bigr)^\top$. That vector is the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space. The projections lesson derives the same point from the normal equations; the identities $P^2=P=P^\top$ stay here.

traps: Using $P=A(AA^\top)^{-1}A^\top$. The Gram matrix in the middle is $A^\top A$, which is $n\times n$ when $A$ is $m\times n$ with independent columns. Swapping the order asks a different matrix to be invertible.
Dropping the inverse and writing $P=AA^\top$ when the columns are not orthonormal. For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $AA^\top$ is twice the correct $P$.
Quoting $P^2=P$ and forgetting symmetry. A non-symmetric idempotent matrix has eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ and trace equal to rank, and it is still not an orthogonal projection.
Thinking every eigenvalue of a projection has absolute value $1$. That is the orthogonal-matrix fact. A projection of rank less than the ambient dimension has $0$ as an eigenvalue.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

M = [[1, 1, 0], [1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
assert mul(M, M) == [[2, 2, 0], [2, 2, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
N = [[2, -1, 1], [-1, 2, 1], [1, 1, 2]]
assert mul(N, N) == [[3 * x for x in row] for row in N]
assert all(N[i][j] == N[j][i] for i in range(3) for j in range(3))
assert sum(N[i][i] for i in range(3)) == 6
b = [1, 1, 0]
Nb = [sum(N[i][j] * b[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)]
assert Nb == [1, 1, 2]
print(2)

questions.stem: The columns of $A$ are linearly independent. The orthogonal projection matrix onto the column space of $A$ is
options: $AA^\top$, whether or not the columns are orthonormal
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. Full column rank makes $A^\top A$ invertible, and $P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$ is symmetric and idempotent with image equal to the column space. Option B puts the factors in an order that need not even be defined as an inverse of an $n\times n$ Gram matrix. Option D is the special case $A^\top A=I$ only.

The answer is **B**. Orthogonal projection means symmetric and idempotent, written $P^2=P=P^\top$. Option A is a reflection or a rotation-type equation, not a projection. Option C is the orthogonal-matrix equation $Q^\top Q=I$. Eigenvalues of $P$ are $0$ or $1$, so a proper projection has an eigenvalue whose absolute value is not $1$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of every orthogonal projection matrix $P$?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The polynomial $x(x-1)$ annihilates $P$, so the only eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$, and the trace equals the multiplicity of $1$, which is the rank. Symmetry is part of $P^2=P=P^\top$. D fails as soon as $0$ is an eigenvalue: then $\det P=0$, so $P$ cannot satisfy $P^\top P=I$ unless $P=I$.

questions.stem: Let $P=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. If $M$ is the integer matrix inside $P$, then $M^2=2M$, so $P^2=P$. The matrix is symmetric and its diagonal sums to $\tfrac12+\tfrac12+0=1$. The eigenvalues are $1,0,0$: explicitly $P(1,1,0)^\top=(1,1,0)^\top$ and $P$ kills $(1,-1,0)^\top$ and $(0,0,1)^\top$. The value $3$ is not among them.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Enter $\mathrm{trace}(P)$, where $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of $A$.
questions.solution: The answer is **2**. The two columns of $A$ are linearly independent, so $\mathrm{rank}(A)=2$ and the projection onto the column space has the same rank. For an orthogonal projection, $\mathrm{trace}(P)=\mathrm{rank}(P)$, hence the trace is $2$. The explicit matrix is $\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&1\\-1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose diagonal sums to $2$.
